Uniform Title: Nirvāṇayogottara Manuscript: BHU C4246 Notes: Data entered by the staff of Muktabodha under the supervision of Mark S.G. Dyczkowski.
Revision 0: April 7, 2012 Country of Publication: India The water, being repeatedly agitated by the wind as it moves, [is stirred].
Since there is no such thing as immobility, it is likewise difficult to find such a thing as "mind. || 1 ||
Oṃ! Blessed One, Lord of the gods of gods, Protector of the world, Master of the universe:
please explain in brief the cause by which the mind becomes perfectly steady. (2)
Excellent, excellent, O one of great wisdom! Your skill of intellect has been observed.
I shall speak, without doubt, especially out of affection for my son. (3)
The cause is said to be threefold: that which is gross, subtle, and supreme.
By the gross [cause], the gods are colored and Mahāmāyā is brought under control. (4)
But I shall declare the cause; listen with one-pointed mind, O Guha:
within the middle of the palate is the instrument (karaṇa), which is devoid of inhalation and exhalation.
Situated between the navel, the heart, and the region of the throat, the *kanda* is slightly bent;
it is known as the palate because from it [the breath] moves upward.
When the intellect is fixed upon that place, it becomes wonderfully and perfectly steady;
and when the mind is motionless, then the vision proceeds.
And that vision, perceivable by others, beholds the three worlds in an instant;
then, the unattainable is attained and the imperceptible is perceived.
Abiding in the middle between inhalation and exhalation, with the manifest and the unmanifest perfectly stilled,
sleep then proceeds for one who is devoted to yoga and meditation.
He who consumes bliss born from the nectar of immortality experiences a state that proceeds as non-bliss, unmoving, and free from all attributes. (10)
It is beyond comparison, without appearance, and free from meditation and dhāraṇīs;
having made one's vision empty, one should then perceive that very emptiness. || 11 ||
Empty, empty, and again empty—this is called the triple emptiness in an instant;
then all is empty, without appearance, and there arises the state of essential equality. || 12 ||
Just as ghee poured into ghee, or likewise milk into milk,
when oneness has been attained, one should not think of anything at all.
Having abandoned breaths that are free from desire and characterized by exhalation, the inhalation (pūraka) becomes nectar-like;
and when the retention (kumbhaka) is performed by yogis through the concentration of yoga, it is so described.
Where cessation arises, everything proceeds as empty;
that which is situated within the empty remains like space within space. (15)
Neither red nor yellow, neither white nor black;
liberated from all qualities, it transcends all states, being both supreme and non-supreme. (16)
You have spoken of inhalation (pūraka) and retention (kumbhaka) again and again;
I bow to that God who is difficult to attain—how can human beings know him? (17)
Having performed inhalation with the breath and then retention like a water-jar, this is indeed the illusory power (māyā) created, O child, by which living beings are deluded. (18)
Having performed this breath-retention (kumbhaka), one should perceive that which resides within the body at the location of the heart as being devoid of form; it is never external.
All this is called the supreme *pūraka*;
it is like space arisen therein, free from any fixed location. (20)
"O son, speak thus: 'This is peaceful,' and [speak] this independently.
The mudrā is performed by Nandin; there, the lips are pressed together. (21)
Having meditated upon Śiva, one should not think of anything else, even for a moment;
I am satisfied, O great enjoyer. Thus has it been told to you according to my own authority. (22)
One should repeatedly contemplate that which is beyond me, supremely peaceful, free from the web of speech, and declared to be the junction of my own being. (23)
And here, O one with eyes for what is beneficial, meditation upon non-existence is of great significance;
otherwise, O lady of great fortune, I am unable [to attain it] even in hundreds of lifetimes. (24)
One should meditate upon that supreme bliss which is described as one's own self by the Vedas—eternal, called the void, the void of the heart, devoid of form. (25)
It has no station within the body, nor ever outside;
everything proceeds as that which is called "equal flavor," devoid of any ultimate foundation.
When others have dissolved into emptiness, their own essential nature is no longer found;
the mind, intellect, and ego remain like a thorn in a mango fruit.
The sense faculties are empty, yet they have dissolved into the supreme emptiness; when one has merged into the supreme emptiness, one's own nature is no longer perceived at all. (28)
Even amidst the sounds of musical instruments, the clamor of drums, and the tumultuous noise of the people,
the mind of one who is proficient in the reality of yoga is not disturbed.
"O child, I have made a bond of the place, meditation, and the moving and non-moving;
for that which is absolute, how could there be a place? No meditation exists for it. (30)
Since there is no such thing as concentration (dhāraṇā) and so forth, everything is empty and devoid of qualities;
and having repeatedly pierced through that which is devoid of qualities, it has been made manifest by me.
By his own will, he completely severed that thing called "rasa" on all sides,
just as a heroic archer draws a shaft back to his ear.
Having pierced the target, the yogi who is thus devoted to the True Being likewise pierces only the target;
he perceives neither the bow, nor the arrow, nor the target, nor even the person.
Having thus known the supreme reality, which stands in the sky like the sky itself, one should fill another section [of the body] and remain with the gaze fixed upon the pillar. (34)
When this reality is attained, one should not think of anything at all—neither mind nor intellect, neither place nor even color. (35)
There is neither meditation nor the object of meditation, neither the knot nor the vital air; there is neither the thread nor the knotted cord, neither the drop nor the sound.
There is neither the object of perception nor the perceiver, neither the crest nor the fourth state itself;
when one has reached that middle between them, one should not think of anything at all.
Neither wind nor space, nor fire nor water likewise;
neither the moon nor the sun, nor even Brahmā or Viṣṇu. (38)
Neither Rudra, nor Kāla, nor Īśvara, nor Śiva; neither the Ineffable, nor the Effulgence-less, nor that which is beyond the principles (nirātman), nor the Support-less. || 39 ||
Concealed, all-pervading, peaceful, and situated like space within spaces—then something begins to manifest as one perceives it again and again. (40)
Having again performed that measurement, the gross [element] dissolves into the void;
when the subtle void is reached, it dissolves into the supreme void. (41)
When that auspicious state has been attained—which is motionless and likewise devoid of qualities—one should fix the mind right there, for there is no other cause [for liberation]. (42)
This is that supreme limit and likewise the supreme mind;
this is that supreme intellect and it proceeds as the highest.
From that, the question of the yogi falls away; of this there is no doubt.
"Viṣṇu knows this": by means of wrath, the bond is severed.
Because he is the god who is honored by all the great gods, he is celebrated as Mātṛvadeva;
and because he delivers all his subjects, he is called Tumburu.
Even so, because he possesses lordship (īśvaratva), he is proclaimed as Īśvara;
because he removes all sins, the god is proclaimed as Hara. || 46 ||
The refuge of all beings is called the *liṅga* because it is their refuge;
thus, the omnipresent God is not stainless in the form of Brahman. || 47 ||
Whatever consists of speech—among worms, insects, and moths, among the stationary and the moving—is all proclaimed to have the Lord of Creation as its deity. (48)
The power of that god beyond gods vibrates throughout the universe;
thus, one should perceive the all-pervading void within the heart. (49)
O Lord, if you say that everything is all-pervading and empty, then what is it called?
Furthermore, if emptiness is the characteristic of the Supreme Brahman, how can there be any apprehension [of it]? 50.
O Blessed One, Lord of the gods of gods, whose crest is adorned with the crescent moon;
O Wielder of the Trident, grant grace regarding this supreme secret question.
By means of the six-limbed yoga, one should cause the heart to grasp emptiness;
through that, one should perceive the fullness of the turning back and the state of fullness.
Then, when the time for initiation has arrived, one should offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti).
With his self purified through yoga, he shall attain perfection and reach the state of moving through the sky (khecaratā). || 53 ||
Prāṇāyāma, as well as dhyāna, pratyāhāra, dhāraṇā, tarka, and samādhi—this is said to be the six-limbed yoga. || 54 ||
This is declared to be composed of knowledge; the object of knowledge is proclaimed to be emptiness.
From that, the sense faculties are empty, and the mind is likewise empty. (55)
One should know it to be devoid of intellect, and then likewise devoid of the self;
having made it devoid of fire, one should then make it devoid of dharma and partless.
Smokeless and supremely empty, like water within a jar,
it becomes colorless and motionless when the winter season has arrived.
In this way, one should apply [the syllables] Khaṃ, Kāṣṭha, Dhū, and likewise Kha and Tiṣṭha.
When this reality is attained, one sees that there is no birth from bondage. 58.
Furthermore, non-duality can never arise for a householder, because he is attached to the sense organs, and being so attached, he is likewise possessed by envy. (59)
Ignorance causes passion and dispassion to seize the mind again and again;
therefore, that mind from which reality has not been won does not turn away from them.
When the mind has been conquered, then the highest good proceeds;
one who is peaceful, self-controlled, with anger subdued, subsisting on alms, and free from longing.
But having seen this, the yogin should strive with great effort;
by seeing it, one is liberated from sin, and by touching it, one becomes initiated.
O Skanda, through conversation, contact, eating together, and sharing a bed or seat,
such a person brings ruin to ten preceding and ten succeeding generations of their family.
The matured [state] is indeed the Pratijñāna, and the Ghaṭikā is fourfold:
the first is the division of dust (dhūlibheda), and the second is the binding that cuts the heart (hṛcchedabandhana).
The third is the breaking of the knot, and the fourth is said to be supreme.
How do they grasp that state merely through the awakening of the mind? (65)
By what is the mind grasped, and in what place does it dissolve?
O God of gods, Great God, you who discern the meaning of all principles! (66)
Tell me the supreme knowledge by which practitioners attain accomplishment.
Chalk (khaṭikā) is said to be liberation; one should extract it through the breaking of knots.
Having known the supreme as being like space (kha), this is proclaimed as "chalk" (khaṭikā). 67.
Having withdrawn the mind into the mind, and likewise the intellect into the intellect, that intellect—following the path of reality—is to be known as supreme. (68)
Listen to the characteristic of emptiness: at that very moment, one enters into the support;
and once the supreme reality has been entered, equanimity arises in an instant. (69)
When equanimity is attained, supreme bliss arises;
when supreme bliss is attained, one should not think of anything at all. (70)
The practitioner, having become absorbed in that [state], should enter by means of the seed-syllable of Śiva;
at that time, the sound of conchs, kettledrums, or large drums is no longer heard.
And being struck, it would not feel pain, for it has become one with that [blow].
This is your supreme secret; it is the highest object of knowledge, without a doubt.
Having encountered this very condition, that Guru becomes a destroyer of bonds (pāśahā), he who performs initiation by means of a flower, a leaf, a fruit, or water. (73)
Therefore, he performed the sacrifice with nine naves; of this there is no doubt.
If one performs the initiation otherwise, that guru becomes a slayer of a Brahmin.
Likewise, O Śiva, those great fools who [cling to] duality in meditation suffer again and again in saṃsāra without end. (75)
Duality, great duality, and likewise the unity of duality;
from the perspective of ultimate reality, my mind perceives neither non-duality nor duality. (76)
O Maheśvara, by your grace, may my lineage, whose name is unknown, become renowned;
what kind of great chariot shall it be, and what indeed shall the matted locks be like? (77)
O Lord of Gods, tell me briefly: what is that which is produced called *bhāsa*, or what is meant by the *khaṭvāṅga*, by means of which liberation becomes certain? (78)

One should meditate upon the other [emptiness], which is void, infinite, and devoid [of all things]; it is the tranquil, supreme state that brings about the cessation of existence—why is it called "the other"? (79)
One should bathe the mind as if it were matted hair; for these are proclaimed to be the matted locks.
That is declared the "Great Bath," and that is called the "Great Vow. (80)
There is no supreme bliss that is mental or devoid of mind;
therefore, one should remain like a piece of wood in space, for such is the khaṭvāṅga. || 81 ||
Thus one should understand it as hidden; likewise, one is called a "dweller in the cave.
One is not liberated by the mere utterance of a name, nor is one pure simply because the body is free from impurity. (82)
The wise one quiets the mind; this is designated as "liberation.
Having performed the observance of the vow, one should practice yoga therein. (84)
By me, the Supreme Brahman, which transcends the three worlds, was realized in the past. || 85 ||
O Maheśvara, you yourself have declared that yogas are accompanied by vows;
those who are devoid of yoga, though adorned with the five mudrās, are merely fools observing vows. (86)
Explain this doubt of mine, so that I may become free from uncertainty. || 87 ||
Yogas accompanied by vows are all auspicious and bestow perfection;
however, fools who possess vows but lack yoga are never liberated.
Having performed the observance of his vow, free from worldly concerns, he is eternally desireless toward the desireless, regarding a clod of earth, a stone, and gold as equal. (89)
Sound, touch, taste, form, and smell as the fifth—by these great mudrās, the fourfold world is liberated. (90)
Thus liberated, one should go to liberation where the stainless God resides.
I bow to the venerable, all-encompassing, and supreme mother.
May it be auspicious.
